# Switch

An on/off setting that takes effect the moment it moves.

```tsx
import { Switch } from "@rata/react";
```

| | |
|---|---|
| Registry name | `switch` |
| Family | inputs |
| Tier | free |
| Status (css / react / figma) | latest / latest / future |
| Depends on | `state-layer`, `visually-hidden` |

## Behavior

A native input[type=checkbox] carrying role="switch". The platform supplies Space-to-toggle, the checked state and form participation; the role changes only how it is announced — "Notifications, on" rather than "Notifications, checked".

Headless contract: `getSwitchProps` in `packages/primitives/src/switch.ts` — importable from `@rata/primitives` without the React wrapper or any CSS.

- **A setting, not a value waiting to be submitted** — This is the whole reason the component exists separately from Checkbox. A checkbox is a value you are about to submit with a form; a switch takes effect the moment it moves. Getting this wrong is worse than a styling mistake: a switch beside a Save button promises something the control does not do.
- **role="switch" on a native checkbox, not a div** — The role is the only thing that has to change. Rebuilding the keyboard handling, the checked state and the form participation on a div is how a switch ends up not announcing its state, and there is nothing to gain from it.
- **No indeterminate state** — A setting is on or off. "Partly on" is not a state a system can be in — a parent summarising children that disagree is a Checkbox, which has exactly that state for exactly that reason.
- **The label does not change with the state** — aria-checked already says which way it is set. Swapping the label to "Turn off notifications" means the name and the state contradict each other, and a screen reader announces "Turn off notifications, on" — a double negative the user has to unpick. The same rule toggle-button follows.
- **Activation is guarded, not disabled** — As everywhere in this system: aria-disabled plus a refused activation, so the switch stays focusable and keeps announcing which way it is set. readOnly is no help — it has no effect on a checkbox.

### `label`

```ts
label: ReactNode
```

The setting's label. Always required — `labelHidden` can take it off screen, but nothing removes it.

Source doc: The setting's label. Always required — `labelHidden` hides it, nothing removes it.

**Use when**

- Always. Name the setting, not the action: "Notifications", not "Turn on notifications".

**Don't use for**

- A label that changes with the state. `aria-checked` says which way it is set, so a label that also says it produces "Turn off notifications, on".
- Passing an empty string. An unnamed switch is a control nobody can describe; hide it with `labelHidden` instead.

**Accessibility** A real `<label for>` bound to the input, so the text is part of the hit target.

### `labelHidden`

```ts
labelHidden?: boolean
```

Takes the label off screen while leaving it in the accessibility tree.

**Use when**

- A row in a settings table whose column already names the setting.

**Don't use for**

- A standalone switch. With nothing else naming it, the label is the only thing saying what is being turned on.

**Accessibility** Clipped, not `display: none` — the label element is still rendered and still bound, so the accessible name is unchanged.

### `checked`

```ts
checked?: boolean
```

Whether the setting is on. Makes the component controlled.

**Use when**

- Whenever the setting lives outside the component, which for a setting is essentially always.

**Don't use for**

- Passing it without `onCheckedChange`; the switch would render its state and refuse to change it.
- Flipping it optimistically when the change is a server round trip that can fail — the switch would be lying about the setting.

**Conflicts with** `defaultChecked`

**Accessibility** Drives `aria-checked`, which is announced as on/off rather than checked/unchecked.

### `defaultChecked`

```ts
defaultChecked?: boolean
```

Starting state for an uncontrolled switch.

Source doc: Starting state for an uncontrolled switch. Conflicts with `checked`.

**Use when**

- A local view preference nothing else on the page reads.

**Conflicts with** `checked`

### `onCheckedChange`

```ts
onCheckedChange?: (checked: boolean, event: { preventDefault(): void }) => void
```

Called with the state the setting should move to.

**Use when**

- Applying the change immediately — that is what makes this a switch rather than a checkbox.

**Don't use for**

- Deferring the effect to a Save button. If the change needs saving, the control is a Checkbox.

### `description`

```ts
description?: ReactNode
```

Helper text under the label, for a setting whose consequence is not obvious.

Source doc: Helper text under the label.

**Use when**

- Saying what turning it on actually does, when the label alone cannot.

**Don't use for**

- Restating the label in more words.

### `id`

```ts
id?: string
```

Stable id for the input. Defaults to a generated one.

### `disabled`

```ts
disabled?: boolean
```

Blocks the change while keeping the switch focusable and readable.

**Use when**

- A setting that cannot be changed yet but whose current state still matters to see.

**Don't use for**

- Expressing "off". Disabled and off are different facts, and a disabled switch can be either.

**Accessibility** Emits `aria-disabled` and refuses activation. Never the native `disabled` attribute.

### `className`

```ts
className?: string
```

Class for the switch's wrapper.

**Don't use for**

- Restyling the track or thumb — those are the approved token mapping.

## Use cases

### A setting that applies immediately

The canonical case, and the only one this component is for.

```tsx
<Switch
  label="Notifications"
  checked={notifications}
  onCheckedChange={setNotifications}
/>
```

The label names the setting, not the action. `aria-checked` says which way it is set, so "Notifications" is announced as "Notifications, on" — which is what a setting sounds like.

### A setting whose consequence needs saying

Where the label alone cannot explain what turning it on does.

```tsx
<Switch
  label="Public profile"
  description="Anyone with the link can see your activity."
  checked={isPublic}
  onCheckedChange={setPublic}
/>
```

### A row in a settings table

Where the column heading already names the setting.

```tsx
<Switch label="Email digest" labelHidden checked={row.digest} onCheckedChange={…} />
```

`labelHidden` hides the pixels, not the name — each row is still announced with what it controls.

### Reaching for the wrong component

The change is not applied until a form is submitted.

```tsx
<Switch label="Email me updates" checked={draft.email} onCheckedChange={setDraft} />
<Button>Save changes</Button>
```

Don't. A switch beside a Save button promises something it does not do: it says the setting took effect, and it did not. That is a Checkbox — a value you are about to submit. The distinction is the entire reason both components exist.

## Real usage in this repo

```tsx
<Switch label="Push digest" labelHidden />
```

## Token recipe

### base

A track the thumb slides along. The track's fill is the state, and the thumb's position says the same thing a second way, so the setting is never carried by colour alone.

| Property | Token |
|---|---|
| track inline-size | `size.control.lg — the track is twice the thumb's diameter plus its inset, which is what gives the thumb somewhere to travel; borrowing a control step keeps it on the scale` |
| track block-size | `size.icon.md — the same height as a checkbox's box, so a switch and a checkbox in one settings column line up` |
| track border-radius | `radius.pill` |
| track background (off) | `theme.bg.muted — the most recessed surface, so an off switch reads as an empty channel rather than a filled control` |
| track background (on) | `theme.accent-role.bg` |
| track border | `border.default solid theme.border.strong when off — an off track needs its own boundary at the 3:1 WCAG 1.4.11 asks of a control's edge, because its fill is nearly its surroundings. On, the accent fill is the boundary and the border matches it` |
| thumb size | `space.gap.lg — a spacing step rather than the icon scale, because the thumb is a mark and not a glyph, the same reasoning the radio's dot follows. At 16px it fills 89% of the track's inner height, which is the proportion a switch reads as; smaller and it looks like a dot rattling in a channel` |
| thumb border-radius | `radius.pill` |
| thumb background (off) | `theme.fg.secondary` |
| thumb background (on) | `theme.fg.on-accent — the only foreground permitted on the accent fill, and it inverts with the accent in the dark scheme` |
| thumb inset | `space.0-5 at both ends of the travel — tighter than the checkbox's inset on purpose, since a large thumb wants a couple of pixels of channel showing rather than a gutter` |
| thumb travel | `transform, not a layout property: the thumb slides rather than reflowing, so nothing around it moves` |
| gap between track and label | `space.gap.sm` |
| gap between label and description | `none — the label and the description each carry line-height leading, which already reads as 7px of separation. A gap on top of that made 11px and read as two unrelated lines` |
| label color | `theme.fg.primary` |
| label font-size | `type.control.size.md` |
| description color | `theme.fg.secondary` |
| description font-size | `type.supporting.size` |
| hover/press | `compose the .rata-state-layer class` |
| outline (focus-visible) | `focus.ring-width solid theme.focus-ring, offset focus.ring-offset — drawn on the track, and the offset is kept: a pill this small has no room for a flush ring to read as separate from its own edge` |
| opacity (aria-disabled) | `state.disabled-opacity` |
| transition | `motion.interactive.duration with motion.interactive.easing, on the thumb's transform and the track's fill` |
